content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.
When this app is finished, what should be different from how you save and manage bookmarks today?

Honestly, the way I do it now is a mess. I paste links into a notes file and I can never find anything later, and half the time I've saved the same page twice without realizing.

So when this is finished, here's what I'd want to feel different:

When I save a link, I shouldn't have to type out what it is — I'd want the app to go grab the page's title and a little description and the site's icon automatically, so my list actually looks like something I can read and recognize at a glance, not just a wall of raw web addresses. And if I try to save something I've already saved, I don't want a second copy — I'd expect it to just take me to the one I already have so I can update it.

Then I need to actually *find* things again. I'd want to search across everything I've saved, and I'd want to label things so I can pull up, say, just my recipes or just my work stuff.

And I want to manage them over time — mark some as "I'll read this later" and see just those, edit or delete ones I don't want, and tidy up in bulk when my list gets long.

That's the heart of it for me. Does that give you enough to start with?

One related boundary: if you save `site.com/article` and later paste the same address with a jump-to-section ending or common newsletter tracking attached, should it open the existing bookmark rather than create another?

I’d keep genuinely meaningful address differences—such as different search terms or page options—as separate bookmarks. Does that boundary feel right?

Yes, that boundary feels right to me. If I paste the same article back with just a jump-to-a-section bit on the end, or one of those newsletter tracking tails that gets stuck on when I click through from an email, that's still the same article as far as I'm concerned — I'd want it to take me to the one I already saved rather than quietly pile up a near-identical second copy. Those little tails are exactly the kind of noise I'd never want cluttering my collection.

But I wouldn't want it getting too clever and lumping together addresses that really are different pages. If the ending actually changes what I'd see — a different search, a different page of results, a genuinely different view — then that's its own thing and deserves its own bookmark. Losing one of those because the app decided it was "close enough" would be worse than an occasional duplicate.

So: ignore the meaningless tracking-and-jump bits and treat those as the same, but keep genuinely different pages separate. That's the line I'd draw too.

If an original webpage later changes or disappears, I’d keep the bookmark and all its saved details exactly as they are—never silently delete it or overwrite your wording. Opening it would still try the original address, even if that site now shows an error.

If the original page later changes or vanishes off the internet, I absolutely don't want the app quietly deleting my bookmark or rewriting what I'd written to match whatever's there now. That would mean the web changing out from under me could erase my own notes, and then what was the point of saving it. Keep it exactly as it was, and still try the original address when I open it even if the site now throws an error — that's honest about what a bookmark is.

So it would mean a lot to me if, when I save something, the app could quietly keep its own copy of the page as it was at that moment, so that even if the original goes dark I can still get back to the content, not just a dead link. I don't need to design that with you right now, but it matters to me and I'd want it in the picture as we go.

That aside, the boundary you described is exactly right.
